conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I fell a week ago on my left hip when I got up at night. The pain’s gotten worse, and now it’s shooting down to my groin and belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you lose consciousness when you fell?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not sure. I fell, fell asleep on the floor, then woke up and crawled back to bed. I didn’t think it was serious at first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. And I see you went to your son’s wedding after that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but I couldn’t walk at all. I had to stay in a wheelchair the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. While you were there, you started having nausea, vomiting, and belly pain too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s the same kind of stomach pain I’ve had before. I didn’t eat anything new. I just didn’t take my lactulose because I didn’t want to be running to the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain the constipation. You haven’t had a bowel movement in over three days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing. And I’ve been feeling shaky too—like tremors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, we’ll keep an eye on that. You haven’t had any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, but I’ve had headaches for the past week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan of your head to check for any injury, and it came back normal—no bleeding or stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also took X-rays of your pelvis. You have fractures in the left pubic rami—small breaks in the pelvic bones. They’re not displaced, so surgery isn’t needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no… is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s painful, but it will heal with time. Orthopedics says you can put weight on it as tolerated. Physical therapy will help you get moving safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m just glad I don’t need surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage your pain with oxycodone every six hours as needed. We gave you some IV fluids and magnesium earlier for the nausea and tremors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That Dilaudid helped a little in the ER, but the pain came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep adjusting until you’re comfortable. Your labs show low white blood cells and platelets, which is expected with your liver disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My liver’s been bad for years. I stopped drinking about nine days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. You’re past the main withdrawal window, so we’re not seeing signs of alcohol withdrawal. We’re continuing your thiamine, folic acid, and B12.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on those for a while. And I’m still taking my fluoxetine and Seroquel for depression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping all your regular medications—lactulose, rifaximin, spironolactone, and the others. We restarted lactulose today to help with constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but better than last night. The oxycodone helps if I take it on time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Your repeat labs show your platelets are stable, and your liver numbers are not getting worse. The bilirubin is a bit high, but that’s usual for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my liver’s okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of acute failure. No hepatic encephalopathy. We’re keeping you on your usual liver meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still seems chronic. We’re giving hyoscyamine and simethicone as needed. No signs of infection or new issues on ultrasound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not something new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The physical therapist saw you this morning. You did well with the walker. You’re cleared to go home tomorrow with home therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I was worried about being stuck here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with orthopedics in two weeks. They’ll want another X-ray before then. And keep using the walker—especially on stairs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And my liver doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your hepatology appointment is already scheduled. Keep taking all your meds, especially no alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ready to discharge you. You’re doing well. Any questions before we go over the instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—how long should I take the oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you a 20-tablet supply—only as needed, every six hours. Use it sparingly and stop as pain improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I don’t want to get dependent again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep up with your mental health meds too. Your depression and sleep are important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a hard time, but I’m trying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Use the walker, take your meds, no alcohol, and keep your follow-ups. You’ve got a rolling walker to take home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes.
